title: Restoring a tarnished silver or gilt picture frame
subtitle: Clean tarnish and grime from a silver-leaf or water-gilt picture frame and revive the surface with a specialist gilding wax
excerpt: How to restore a tarnished silver or gilt picture frame. Covers dusting the frame, cleaning surface dirt, applying gilding wax to revive the lustre, buffing to the correct sheen, and working into carved detail.
sourceNotes: Traditional gilding conservation and frame restoration practice, public domain. UK frame restoration trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A traditional gilding technique in which real gold or silver leaf is applied over a gesso and bole base, wetted with water so the leaf adheres by suction, and then burnished to a high reflective polish. Water-gilt surfaces are fragile: cleaning products, abrasive polishes, and even finger contact can remove the leaf. The substrate under the leaf is gesso, which is water-soluble.

A pigmented wax-based product, most commonly sold as Liberon or similar brands, used to touch up worn, chipped, or tarnished gilt surfaces. It deposits a thin layer of metallic pigment in wax that can be burnished to a close approximation of the original gilded surface. It is not a substitute for re-gilding but is very effective for surface tarnish, minor chips, and dullness.

The discolouration on metallic leaf surfaces caused by oxidation and sulphide compounds from the atmosphere. On silver leaf it appears as a dark or grey patchy film. On gold and gilded surfaces it manifests as dullness and a darkening of the reflective surface. Tarnish is usually superficial and can be removed or masked without disturbing the underlying leaf.

Use a clean, soft-bristle brush to dust the frame, working into all carved and moulded details. Compressed air (a photographic dust blower or a can of compressed air) clears dust from deep recesses without physical contact. Do not use a vacuum cleaner nozzle directly on a water-gilt surface: suction can lift fragile leaf.

Dampen a cotton wool ball with a small amount of white spirit and wipe the flat frame surfaces very gently to remove grease and smoke deposits. Do not press hard, do not use water (it will dissolve the gesso under the leaf), and do not use chemical silver polish or abrasive cleaners on gilded surfaces. Test on a hidden section of the rabbet edge before cleaning the visible face.

Apply a very small amount of gilding wax to a fingertip or lint-free cloth. Work it into the frame surface in small sections with a light circular motion. The wax is concentrated: a thin layer is more effective than a thick one. Work into carved details by pressing the tip of a soft cloth or a clean brush into the recesses.

Once the wax has dried for five to ten minutes, buff the treated sections with a clean, dry lint-free cloth using light strokes. The wax produces a moderate sheen rather than a bright mirror polish. Repeat the application on any areas where the original gilding was dark or heavily worn. Do not over-buff water-gilt sections: hard rubbing can remove the underlying leaf.

attrs.symptom: Gilding wax leaves a smeared, uneven sheen
attrs.cause: Too much wax was applied, or it was buffed before fully drying.
attrs.fix: Apply a very thin second coat of wax over the streaky area and buff again when fully dry, using a clean cloth.

attrs.symptom: Areas of the frame show white gesso through the gilding even after treatment
attrs.cause: The original gilding has worn through in those areas and no surface treatment will fully cover it.
attrs.fix: Apply gilding wax to reduce the contrast. For larger worn areas, apply genuine gold or silver size and leaf for a permanent repair.
